location.title: Find the dojo before your first visit.
location.copy: RenshinKan Dojo is in Baan Waen, Hang Dong. Parents and visitors can use the map to plan arrival, then message ahead so the dojo can confirm the best class time and where to observe.

visiting.title: Drop-ins are always welcome.
visiting.copy: If you're new, feel free to come along. Just turn up at class time. If you're a visiting aikidoka, we'd love a quick message ahead so we can make sure the timing works and someone can greet you properly.

intro.title: A welcoming place to start, grow, and keep showing up.
intro.copy: Everyone is welcome here, from complete beginners and children to experienced aikidoka passing through Chiang Mai. Each session is 90 minutes and has two parts. The first half is for beginners and kids, and the second half is for intermediate students, adults, and weapons practice. Drop in anytime or reach out first if you have questions.
intro.imageAlt: Students in white uniforms lying in a circle on the mat with green belts in the centre.

halves.firstCopy: The opening portion of every class is designed for beginners and children. Safe falling, basic posture, footwork, and partner awareness at a measured pace.
halves.secondCopy: The second portion moves into more demanding technique work, combinations, partner drills, and weapons practice suited to adults and students who are ready to push further.

schedule.title: Four sessions a week, every week.
schedule.copy: Tuesday and Thursday evenings, Saturday and Sunday mornings. Each class runs for 90 minutes and follows the same two-part structure: beginners first, then all levels.
schedule.imageAlt: Weekly class schedule: Tuesday and Thursday 17:30-19:00, Saturday and Sunday 9:00-10:30

firstVisit.title: A calm first class starts with a few simple steps.
firstVisit.copy: This guide is for beginners, parents, and visiting aikidoka. Message ahead so we can confirm the right class time and whether to observe or join in.
firstVisit.item1: Drop-ins are welcome, just come along at class time
firstVisit.item2: Message ahead to confirm class time and what to expect
firstVisit.item3: Arrive at least 30 minutes early to help with preparing the dojo
firstVisit.item4: Wear loose trousers and a t-shirt. A keikogi is only needed once you feel ready
firstVisit.item5: Remove shoes before stepping onto the mat, and wash your feet
firstVisit.item6: Let the instructor or a senior student guide you through the bow-in

beltExams.copy: Belt examinations follow the All Dojo Chiang Mai standard under Aikikai affiliation. Progress through the kyu system requires completing the listed techniques and a minimum number of training days at each level. The table below shows what is needed to advance.

experience.question: Do I need experience to join?
experience.answer: Not at all. Everyone is welcome, regardless of background. Aikido is learned from the very beginning, and new students are introduced gradually alongside people at all levels.

age.question: What age is welcome?
age.answer: All ages are welcome at RenshinKan. We have classes for children, teens, adults, and older students. If you are unsure whether a class is the right fit for your age group, just come along and see.

childrenSafety.question: Is aikido safe for children?
childrenSafety.answer: Yes. Aikido is often described as the art of nonviolence. Its techniques are built around blending with force rather than meeting it head on. As long as students take practice seriously and follow the guidance of their instructor, it is a very safe art. Students learn falling, spacing, and partner care gradually, so no one is pushed beyond what they are ready for.

parentsWatch.question: Can parents watch?
parentsWatch.answer: Yes. The dojo has a viewing deck with seating so parents can observe class and get a feel for the tone and rhythm of practice. Parents are also very welcome to join in on the mat themselves. Aikido is a great activity to share as a family.

beginnerClothes.question: What should beginners wear?
beginnerClothes.answer: Comfortable, loose trousers and a T-shirt are perfectly fine for a first visit. There is no need to buy a keikogi right away. Students are only expected to get one when they feel ready and settled in. If you are interested in getting a keikogi, the dojo can help point you in the right direction.

competition.question: Does aikido involve competition?
competition.answer: Aikido has no competitions or tournaments. It is a cooperative martial art. Both partners work together, taking turns as the one who initiates and the one who receives. The goal is to learn timing, balance, and how to move safely with another person, not to win.

falling.question: How do students learn to fall safely?
falling.answer: Students begin with low, careful ukemi practice, learning how to protect the head, soften impact, and move with the floor before techniques become more dynamic.

busySchedule.question: I am very busy. Can I still come?
busySchedule.answer: Yes. Aikido is good exercise and stretching for both the body and the mind, and even one session a week makes a difference. Come every day or just once a week. Whatever your schedule allows. There is no pressure to attend at any fixed frequency.

monthlyFee.question: How much is the monthly dojo upkeep fee?
monthlyFee.answer: The dojo recommends a contribution of 1,500 baht per month to help cover running expenses. Instructors are not paid, and all contributions go directly back into maintaining and running the dojo.

firstVisit.question: How do we arrange a first visit?
firstVisit.answer: Feel free to drop in at any class time. No booking needed. If you prefer to reach out first, you are welcome to contact us ahead of time. Visiting aikidoka are recommended to get in touch before coming so we can make sure the timing works well.

hero.title: What is Aikido?
hero.subtitle: A Japanese martial art of harmony, nonviolence, and lifelong personal growth.

overview.title: What Is Aikido?
overview.intro1: Aikido is a modern Japanese martial art founded in the early twentieth century by Morihei Ueshiba, known to students as O Sensei. Rather than meeting force with force, aikido teaches you to blend with an attack, redirect its energy, and control balance so that conflict can be resolved without relying on brute strength.
overview.intro2: Aikido grew from older Japanese martial traditions, including jujutsu and the classical weapons arts. It also shares qualities with arts such as judo, especially in its attention to balance, throws, and safe falling practice. The result is a practice that values calm, control, and genuine care for a training partner over winning or overpowering an opponent.
overview.weaponsIntro: Weapons practice is not separate from empty hand aikido. Training with traditional wooden weapons teaches distance, timing, posture, center line, awareness, and clear body movement. Many empty hand techniques echo the same principles and movement patterns found in weapons work, especially those of the sword.
overview.bokkenDesc: Used to study posture, cutting lines, and the sword movement that shapes many aikido techniques.
overview.joDesc: Used to develop extension, timing, and smooth, connected footwork.
overview.tantoDesc: Used to practice calm, safe responses, careful distance, and steady awareness.
overview.weaponsClose: Because hand to hand and weapons practice share the same foundation, growth in one naturally deepens understanding of the other. The two sides of aikido constantly support and explain each other.

why.title: Why Pick Aikido?
why.intro: Aikido offers far more than self defense. Regular practice builds qualities that carry into daily life, helping students feel more settled, capable, and aware both on and off the mat.
why.ukemi1: One of aikido's most practical life skills is ukemi, the art of falling and receiving techniques safely. From the very first class, students learn to relax, protect the head, round the body, roll, and land without getting hurt.
why.ukemi2: This matters far beyond the dojo. Slips, trips, everyday accidents, sport, and the natural changes that come with aging all involve falling at some point. Learning to fall well is a real world skill that can genuinely help reduce the risk of injury.
why.close: Aikido is not only about self defense. It is also about learning to move well, stay calm, and respond to pressure without panic or aggression.

who.title: Who Can Practice?
who.intro: Aikido can be practiced by adults, children, complete beginners, and experienced martial artists alike. You do not need to be strong, athletic, flexible, or experienced to begin. Even very senior practitioners, well into older age, are warmly welcome and can keep training at their own pace — it is a wonderful way to stay active, mobile, and flexible as the years go on. Progress comes through steady practice, attention, and learning correct movement rather than relying on physical strength alone.
who.visitorsDesc: Aikidoka passing through Chiang Mai are always welcome to step onto the mat. Send a quick message before you visit so we can confirm the timing and have someone ready to greet you.

about.title: Peace through movement, not force.
about.copy: Aikido is a Japanese martial art founded in the early 20th century by Morihei Ueshiba. It grew from classical traditions including jujutsu, judo, and the sword arts, but took a different direction. Instead of striking or overpowering, aikido teaches you to blend with incoming energy, redirect it, and resolve conflict without causing injury. There is no competition, no aggression. The practice is about composure, self-discipline, and learning to stay calm under pressure.
about.point1Body: Founded by Morihei Ueshiba from classical jujutsu and aiki sword traditions.
about.point2Body: Redirects and neutralises force rather than meeting it. No striking, no competition.
about.point3Body: Builds composure, awareness, and respect. These qualities carry well beyond the mat.
about.traditionCopy: Bokken and jo practice connects aikido to the classical Japanese weapons arts from which it evolved, a living link to centuries of budo.
about.spaceCopy: The kamiza is a focal point of attention in every dojo. It reflects aikido's emphasis on sincerity, respect, and a settled, open mind.

instructors.title: A line of practice rooted in Chiang Mai.
instructors.copy: RenshinKan's instructors trained across Japan, Bangkok, and Chiang Mai, building a teaching line that now welcomes students of all ages and backgrounds.

history.title: From older budo to a living local practice.
history.copy: Each entry marks a period in the full written history told below.
history.storyTitle: O Sensei, aikido, and the path from force to harmony.
history.storyCopy: Aikido means "the way of harmonious spirit," a name that reflects its founding philosophy of blending, not clashing. Its history is not a straight line from violence to gentleness. It is a layered story of older martial skill, spiritual searching, wartime pressure, postwar reconstruction, and ordinary people learning to practice with respect.

intro.title: Aikido as a daily practice of respect, safety, and personal growth.
intro.copy: RenshinKan sits at the centre of a wider network that includes the Peace Culture Foundation, the AikidoCMU university club, and a community of dojos across Chiang Mai. Aikido here isn't just a training system. It's a shared way of learning to move through conflict with calm and care.

foundation.title: The organisation behind RenshinKan's dojo and community mission.
foundation.copy: The Peace Culture Foundation built RenshinKan in 2013 and continues to connect the dojo's training culture to broader work in child safety, grooming prevention, and peaceful conflict resolution across Chiang Mai.
foundation.groomingTitle: Prevention starts with language, boundaries, and trusted adults.

cmu.heroTitle: AikidoCMU: aikido at CMU since around 1986.
cmu.title: Where RenshinKan's lineage began.
cmu.copy1: The founders of RenshinKan, Ajarn Sombat Tapanya and Ajarn Teerarat Boripantakul, both trained at AikidoCMU before establishing RenshinKan Dojo in 2013. The university club has been part of Chiang Mai's aikido community since the mid-1980s, first sharing space with the CMU judo club before growing into its own practice group.
cmu.copy2: AikidoCMU has consistently welcomed CMU students, international students, and community members who train with regular discipline and mutual respect. Their public sessions remain open to anyone serious about practice, so message ahead to confirm current times and location.

monthly.title: This dojo exists because its students take care of it.
monthly.copy1: Every student who trains regularly at RenshinKan is asked to contribute {{amount}}. This is not a membership fee. It is a shared responsibility. The lights, the water, the mats, the repairs, the space itself: all of it is held up by the people who use it.
monthly.copy2: When everyone who trains here contributes, the dojo stays strong for current students, new beginners, and the wider Chiang Mai community.
monthly.noteStrong: Instructors receive no payment from contributions.
monthly.note: Every baht goes directly back into the space you train in.
monthly.supportImageAlt: Students training aikido at RenshinKan Dojo in Hang Dong.
monthly.arrangeCopy: This static website does not process payments or collect payment details. Please arrange contributions directly with the dojo.
monthly.coversCopy: Every baht goes straight back into the dojo. Below is each category your monthly contribution helps cover, from the training hall and mats to weapons, upkeep, events, and the small comforts that keep the space welcoming. Nothing is spent outside this list.
monthly.reminderCopy: Instructors are not compensated from these funds. They teach because they practice, and they practice because they believe in it. The money keeps the lights on.
monthly.whyCopy: Regular contributions let the dojo plan repairs and supplies before something becomes urgent.
